title: Lansing Grand River's 18-month gap is a planning problem, not a closure

chapters.headline: A hole in the calendar, not a closing plant
points: December 17, 2026: the last current-generation Cadillac CT5 comes off the line at Lansing Grand River
The next generation is confirmed for the same plant — not expected until the second half of 2028
Between the dates: roughly 18 months with no car to build, 350 workers facing layoff effective January 14, 2027, and a $1.25 billion retooling program
chapters.takeaway: Coverage has argued about whether the plant is closing. It is not — the useful question is what an 18-month hole actually requires.

chapters.headline: Temporary layoffs, a benefit, and the last vehicle
points: 350 employees at the assembly plant and Lansing Regional Stamping, laid off effective January 14, 2027
The layoffs are temporary: GM expects to call employees back after the changeover, some before the end of 2027
Affected employees may be eligible for transfers, or supplemental unemployment pay equivalent to 74% of their hourly wage under the GM–UAW contract
chapters.takeaway: The CT5 is the plant's last remaining vehicle — the Camaro ended there in December 2023, the CT4 in June 2026.

chapters.headline: What the coverage gets wrong
points: Not a closure — and "18 months idle" is an estimate, not a GM statement; GM has not published a day-by-day account of the retool
The $1.25 billion was redirected, not scrapped: announced in 2023 to convert the plant to EVs, backed by a $500 million federal grant in 2024, now aimed at the gasoline CT5
The 74% is a benefit, not a paycheck — supplemental unemployment pay, with eligibility rules and time limits a paycheck does not have
chapters.takeaway: Each correction changes what the gap means — for the plant, for the program, and for household math.

chapters.headline: Fixed dates, live decisions
points: December 17, 2026: current CT5 production ends; January 14, 2027: layoffs take effect
During 2027: retooling under the $1.25 billion program, with some employees back before the year ends
Second half of 2028: next-generation CT5 production begins — the 2029 model year
chapters.takeaway: Every decision the gap forces — transfer or layoff, wait or train, hold staff or cut — is being made now, on the information available now.

chapters.headline: What 74% actually means
points: Illustrative worker at $35 an hour, 40 hours a week: $1,400 a week gross
At 74%, support is about $1,036 a week — a shortfall of roughly $364 a week, about $1,580 a month
Out a full year, the forgone wages total about $18,900; across the full 18 months, about $28,400
chapters.takeaway: The 74% figure converts a layoff from an emergency into a slow squeeze — survivable with savings, corrosive without, and worse the longer the gap runs.

chapters.headline: A gap planned at a year ran past three
points: Forty miles east, Orion Assembly built the Bolt EV until production ended in December 2023
A $4 billion retool for electric trucks: the start slipped from 2024 to 2025, then to 2026
In June 2025 GM changed the product entirely — gasoline trucks and SUVs instead, production now expected from 2027
chapters.takeaway: Orion's timeline did not fail because the retooling was hard. It failed because the product plan underneath it kept moving — and Lansing's plan has already moved once.

chapters.headline: Judged by conditions stated in advance
points: Going well: GM holds the second-half-2028 restart, first recalls land in 2027, training seats exist and are filled, the stamping plant stays visibly working
Going badly: the restart drifts, "temporary" layoffs are extended or converted, the product changes again, the supplier base visibly thins
The unpriced options: train into the new plant during the layoff window, keep the stamping plant warm, plan for the supplier base — not just the plant
chapters.takeaway: A plant that stops for 18 months is not a crisis. A plant that stops for 18 months without a plan for the interval becomes one — slowly, then all at once at launch.
